Customer Success Guide for AI Companies

Introduction: You’ve Got Customers. Now What?

You had an idea. You built a sweet AI product, and now you have customers. A whole portfolio of them. How cool is that?

But you’re growing, and suddenly it’s hard to give existing clients the CEO-level attention they’ve been used to.

That’s okay! It’s the direction you want your company to go. You just need to hand relationship management to someone else.

That’s where Customer Success (CS) comes in. Customer Success Managers (CSMs) are known to build strong customer relationships, identify growth opportunities, prevent churn, and help customers get the most out of your product. But as you’ll learn, they do so much more.

Who this guide is for. Founders, operators, sales leaders, and heads of Success at AI startups and other AI solution, service, and tech companies. It’s written for a company about to hire its first Success team member, although companies at any stage can use it. Chances are, you already know what Customer Success is. This guide covers how to set it up, including the business case, the role, the processes, the tools, and the habits that keep customers around.

Building a Success team at an AI company comes with a few extra considerations.

AI (artificial intelligence) is booming. New companies, products, and tools show up every day, and businesses in nearly every industry are looking at how they can add AI to their workflows to cut costs and save money. With so many options, customers don’t always know what’s worth investing in, how to use it, or what sets one solution apart.

Some customers are excited. Others are skeptical and worried about what AI means for their business and employees. And in a crazy twist, some may even become your competitors. Not literally. But they may start exploring whether they can build their own alternative instead of paying for yours.

Why retention matters even more for AI companies

Early data suggests AI products lose customers faster than traditional software. The data is young, so read these as directional, not settled.

AI-native vs. traditional SaaS. One analysis (Liat Benzur, March 2026) cites a median annual churn of about 43% for AI-native companies versus about 23% for traditional SaaS, attributed to Datafloq and ChartMogul data. The original figures aren’t published in the article, so treat it as a rough estimate.

Price tier. Focus Digital’s 2026 churn report puts revenue retention for budget AI tools (under $50 a month) as low as 32%, versus 85% for premium AI products (over $250 a month). Its methodology isn’t published either, so read it as a pattern, not a benchmark.

The pattern in both: cheap, easy-to-switch tools churn, and tools tied to real workflows and measurable outcomes stay. That is the job of Customer Success.

A great CSM helps customers cut through the AI noise, build trust, and see why your product is worth paying for. They work for you, while advocating for the customer’s needs.

There are plenty of titles for this role, including Partner Success Manager, Strategic Partner Manager, Enterprise or Technical CSM, Business Relationship Manager, and Client Partner. For simplicity, I’ll use Customer Success Manager throughout this guide.

Whether you’re hiring your first CSM or building an entire department, this guide will help you put the processes, expectations, and tools in place for your team to succeed. Every company has different customers, products, resources, and goals, so take what’s useful and adapt the rest. And be sure to check out the Resources page for useful templates that will turn problems into actionable items.

The guide is in chronological order, following the order you’d actually build things. Make the business case, define the role, map the customer journey, choose your tools, onboard customers and build relationships, and learn from what you find. Read it start to finish, or jump to the step you’re on.

Start here: minimum viable Customer Success

You don’t have to build everything at once. If you only do four things first, do these:

1. Ask five customers, “What does success look like for you?” and write down their answers.

2. Map the customer journey and run the Customer Journey Survey to find your biggest gaps.

3. Write one onboarding outline, and start one Mutual Success Plan and one Customer Health Scorecard for your most important accounts.

4. Hold one business review in a format you can repeat, and record your baseline numbers.

Everything else in this guide can wait until those four are working.

Most of this guide builds on one idea, the customer lifecycle. Here’s the path a customer takes with you, and the stages your CSM will help them through:

Building Your Business Case

Maybe you know you need someone to protect recurring revenue, but you still have to make the case to the people holding the budget.

We know Finance lives by the motto: “If it doesn’t make dollars, it doesn’t make cents.”

Fair enough.

The next two sections get you ready for your elevator pitch and the inevitable Q&A with Finance. Measuring ROI gives you the numbers. Presenting Your Business Case shows you how to use them.

You have a couple of minutes to win someone over. Lead with the benefits, not the cost. Explain how Customer Success protects and grows revenue, improves retention, and creates expansion opportunities. Then show how you’ll measure the team’s return on investment (ROI).

If there’s time, walk through your execution plan, which should include the timeline, resources, and tools you’ll need to get the team up and running.

Know your plan front to back. Once you make the pitch, the questions will come.

Types of questions to be prepared for:

  • What is the cost of doing nothing?
  • How much revenue is at risk today?
  • What does success look like in the first 90 days?
  • How much will it cost to build and operate the team?

Measuring ROI

Just to be clear, Customer Success is not Customer Support.

Your Success team will be a main point of contact for customers. They’ll answer questions, help resolve technical and account-related issues, and make sure customers know where to turn for help. But that’s secondary to their purpose.

Customer Success drives revenue. Period.

The industry increasingly sees it that way, too. In Gainsight’s 2025 Customer Success Index (400+ companies surveyed in September and October 2025), 91% of teams named reducing churn a primary responsibility, 88% named increasing product adoption, and 87% named achieving customer outcomes. Only 19% named customer support, down from 34% in 2023.

Here are the ways your Success team contributes measurable value, and what to track for each:

ContributionWhat the CSM doesWhat to trackExample
Retention and churn preventionSpots risk early, closes adoption gaps, and helps customers see the value they’re gettingGross Revenue Retention (GRR), churn rate, logo retentionA customer whose usage is falling gets retraining and renews instead of canceling
Contract renewals and annual price increasesStarts renewal talks early and explains the value behind the increaseRenewal rate, on-time renewal rate, price increases appliedA customer renews at the contracted 5% increase instead of negotiating it away at the last minute
Expansion revenueFinds new use cases, users, and departmentsNet Revenue Retention (NRR), expansion annual recurring revenue (ARR), expansion pipelineA team that bought for support asks about using the product in sales operations
New business and referralsIdentifies advocates and connects them with SalesReferrals, references, case studies, introductionsA happy customer takes a reference call for a prospect

1. Retention and churn prevention

Keeping an existing customer is generally less expensive than acquiring a new one. CSMs can spot risks before they turn into cancellation requests, address adoption gaps, and help customers understand the value they’re getting.

AI customers have options. They may be comparing multiple tools, questioning whether they need a specialized solution, or wondering if they could build something similar in-house. Protect recurring revenue by giving them a reason to stay.

Retention also drives growth. SaaS Capital’s 2026 survey of more than 1,000 private B2B SaaS companies (2025 results) found median growth of about 15% for companies with NRR of 90% to 100%, 20% at 100% to 110%, 40% at 120% to 130%, and 60% above 130%. Companies with gross retention below 90% reported below-average growth. Note that this simply shows an association between retention and growth, and that the survey covers B2B SaaS in general, not just AI companies.

2. Contract renewals and annual price increases

Renewals are different from retention. If you’ve built annual price increases into your contracts, CSMs can help make sure they’re implemented instead of falling through the cracks.

They make sure your customers are given proper notice so that they have time and space to negotiate. CSMs can provide a clear explanation of the value that will ultimately protect the customer relationship and your company’s revenue.

3. Expansion revenue

As customers grow, their needs change. A CSM who understands their business can spot opportunities for additional products, workflows, users, or use cases.

With AI, those opportunities often sit beyond the department that originally purchased your product. Expansion might mean moving to a higher plan, adopting another product, or finding new ways to get value from your existing solution.

4. New business and referrals

Happy customers can become a source of referrals, introductions, and qualified leads. CSMs can identify potential advocates and connect them with Sales to help generate new business.

There’s even more value than that. Not every contribution from Customer Success shows up as immediate revenue. Some of the team’s most valuable work helps the company in other ways:

  • Testimonials, references, and case studies. Customers who achieve measurable results can become champions of your product. They can help demonstrate your product’s value to prospective buyers. CS can partner with Marketing to find customers willing to share their experiences or act as a reference for new deals.
  • Better product decisions. CSMs hear what customers love, what frustrates them, and what’s getting in the way of value. A consistent feedback loop helps Product and Engineering prioritize improvements that benefit customers.
  • Improved customer experience and operational efficiency. CSMs spot recurring friction across the customer journey, from onboarding to renewal. By working with Support, Product, and Operations to address it, CS can help circumvent issues before they occur.

Presenting Your Business Case

A solid business case does two jobs. It shows Finance the math, and it gives the budget holders something they can repeat to someone else. Numbers get you the meeting. How you present them gets you the budget.

Start with the number Finance cares about

I’d lead with one number, the revenue at risk. It’s the part of your recurring revenue that disappears every year when customers leave. It’s also your cost of doing nothing.

Then give Finance a second number, the break-even point. That’s the share of the at-risk revenue the team has to protect to pay for itself. If you have $5 million in ARR and lose 10% a year, that’s $500,000 walking out the door. A Customer Success hire and tools that cost $150,000 only need to protect 30% of that revenue to break even. Said out loud, it sounds like this: “We lose about $500,000 a year. This costs $150,000. We only have to save three of every ten dollars to cover it.”

How the math works

  • Revenue at risk = the ARR coming up for renewal × your churn rate.
  • Revenue protected = your ARR × the improvement in churn (for example, from 10% to 7% is 3 points).
  • Price increases recovered = the renewing revenue × the annual increase × the share of increases that slip through today.
  • Expansion revenue = the number of expansions you expect × the average expansion size.
  • Return = (total benefit − total cost) ÷ total cost.

Here’s an example with made-up numbers. Say you run Conglom-O, an AI company with $5 million in ARR across 40 customers (about $125,000 each), 10% revenue churn, and a $150,000 annual cost for the role and its tools. Show three scenarios so nobody has to trust one guess.

ConservativeExpectedStretch
Improvement in churn2 points3 points5 points
Revenue protected$100,000$150,000$250,000
Price increases recovered$20,000$20,000$20,000
Expansion revenue$30,000$60,000$90,000
Total benefit$150,000$230,000$360,000
Cost of role and tools$150,000$150,000$150,000
Net return$0+$80,000+$210,000
Return on investment0%53%140%

Illustrative numbers only. Replace them with your own. The Business Case ROI Calculator in the Resources section does this math for you.

Notice that even the conservative case breaks even. That’s a strong thing to be able to say to Finance.

The pitch, in order

  1. The problem. What’s happening to customers and revenue today.
  2. The cost of doing nothing. Your revenue-at-risk number.
  3. The proposal. The role, in one sentence.
  4. The return. Your three scenarios and the break-even point.
  5. The plan and the cost. The first 90 days, the budget, and the tools.
  6. The ask. What you need and by when.

Lead with the benefit, not the ask

I learned this one the hard way. As an account executive, I fought to hire extra beauty advisors for our Sephora and Ulta doors. I knew the extra support would pay off. But I led with the ask, and I wasn’t prepared for the questions that followed. What would it cost? What would we get back? How would we know it worked?

What I should have said sounded more like this: “Ulta Bayfair doesn’t get a lot of support. If we could get someone in there weekly, we could double our numbers there for the rest of the year.” That’s a place, a result, and a timeline. It’s much harder to say no to than “we need more people.”

Do the same here. Start with what Customer Success will protect and grow, then show the cost.

Be ready for the questions

If Finance asks…Answer with…
What is the cost of doing nothing?Your revenue-at-risk number and your current churn rate
How much revenue is at risk today?ARR coming up for renewal in the next 12 months, with the accounts that worry you most
What does success look like in the first 90 days?The first-90-days plan in Mapping Your Customer Journey, with the baseline you’ll measure against
How much will it cost to build and operate the team?Salary and bonus, tools, and any training, in one line
What if churn doesn’t improve?Your conservative case, the date you’ll review results, and what you’ll change if the numbers don’t move

Check your number against a benchmark

Finance will ask whether your number is reasonable. Gainsight’s 2025 index reports median Customer Success spending (people and tools together) as a share of revenue at about 10% for companies under $20 million, 5% for $20 million to $100 million, and 3% above $100 million. The middle half of companies under $5 million spend 5% to 15%.

In the example above, $150,000 against $5 million in ARR is 3% of revenue, well under that median. These are self-reported survey numbers from companies that mostly already have a CS function, so use them as a sanity check, not a target.

Habits that make the pitch land

  • Use your own numbers, even if they’re rough. Say where they came from.
  • Show your math. Finance trusts what it can check.
  • Offer three scenarios instead of one promise.
  • Say what you don’t know yet, and how you’ll find out.
  • Promise to report back on a date, with the same numbers.

Building the Role

There are a million different ways to build a Customer Success team.

Before you ask Claude to build you a CSM job description, take a step back and consider your immediate needs. What problems are you trying to solve? Where are your biggest gaps? And what do you actually need this person to own?

If you can, start with your customers. Ask a handful of them what success looks like for their business and what’s getting in the way. Their answers will tell you more about the role you need than any job description template.

Right now, ask these questions in your head:

  • Are we experiencing significant churn?
  • Are customers struggling to adopt our product or realize its value?
  • Has our customer base grown beyond what the founders can personally manage?
  • Are we missing opportunities to expand existing accounts?
  • Are we struggling to manage renewals consistently?
  • Are internal teams unclear about who owns the customer relationship?
  • Are we spending too much time reacting to customer problems instead of preventing them?
  • Do we have a centralized place to track customer health, manage relationships, and give internal teams visibility into the customer journey?

Your answers will help define the type of CS role you need, its responsibilities, and what success should look like.

And don’t decide this alone. Before you write anything, get the leaders of Sales, Operations, Product, Support, and Marketing together and ask each one: “What does Customer Success mean here, and what do you expect it to own?” Write the answers down. You’ll find out quickly where expectations differ, and everyone will feel part of the decision, which makes them more likely to back it. Churn, renewals, and onboarding touch every team, so Customer Success can’t carry them alone.

How many accounts can one CSM carry? There’s no magic number, and your pricing model changes it. Gainsight’s 2025 index reports about 100 accounts per CSM for subscription pricing in SMB, 50 in mid-market, and 15 in enterprise. Usage-based pricing, which many AI products use, is much lower, at about 23, 20, and 10. Usage swings make accounts less predictable, so CSMs have to watch them more closely.

Average accounts per CSMSubscriptionUsage-based
SMB10023
Mid-market5020
Enterprise1510

Source: Gainsight Customer Success Index 2025. These are survey averages across 400+ companies, not targets. If you price by usage, plan on fewer accounts per CSM than a seat-based benchmark suggests. Most companies use named CSMs (94%), and many also use tech-touch programs (57%) or shared and pooled coverage (45%). Companies can use more than one.

Measuring the Success of Success

You need to track the role’s impact, so it makes sense to define its goals before you hire.

Start with what your customers say success looks like, then choose key performance indicators (KPIs) that reflect the problems you’re trying to solve. If the priority is reducing churn, retention should be a primary measure. If it’s expansion, track expansion revenue.

Use the chart below to connect your business challenges to the metrics that can help measure progress.

If you’re struggling with…Measure success with…
Customer churn and lost revenueGross Revenue Retention (GRR), customer churn rate, renewal rate, logo retention
Retention and expansionNet Revenue Retention (NRR), expansion annual recurring revenue (ARR), upsell and cross-sell revenue, expansion pipeline, and product adoption
Slow onboarding or delayed customer valueTime to Value (TTV), onboarding completion rate, time to first key outcome
Low product adoptionProduct adoption rate, feature utilization, active users, usage frequency
Poor customer experienceCustomer Satisfaction (CSAT), Net Promoter Score (NPS), Customer Effort Score (CES)
Inconsistent renewalsRenewal forecast accuracy, renewal rate, on-time renewal rate

Leading vs. lagging metrics

Renewal rate and churn are lagging metrics. They only tell you what already happened. Onboarding progress, adoption, and value delivered are leading metrics. They move first and predict renewals.

Activity counts, like calls held or emails sent, are useful for managing workload but don’t prove value. More check-ins don’t automatically mean more revenue.

The same index shows how measurement is shifting. Gross Revenue Retention (GRR) is now the most-used revenue metric for CS teams (62%, up from 45% in 2023), while Net Revenue Retention (NRR) slipped to 51%. Teams are increasingly measured on what they directly control, like retention and adoption, with expansion shared more widely.

For a sense of what “good” looks like, the 2026 Aleph and Benchmarkit report (342 B2B SaaS and AI software companies, 2025 data) shows a median NRR of about 102% and a median GRR of about 84%. Companies with usage-based pricing had a median NRR of about 108%, versus about 98% for seat-based pricing, and companies under $5 million in ARR had a median of about 94%. Treat these as rough targets. I’d start with your own baseline and compare it to these once you have a few quarters of data.

You don’t need to measure every metric listed. Start with what makes sense for your business and establish a baseline with realistic targets.

Pay close attention to product adoption. AI is still new, and using it well is becoming a skill in itself. Many customers are still learning, so low usage doesn’t automatically mean you have a bad product. They may just need more guidance or education.

Defining Ownership

Before writing the job description, define what your CSM will own. This may mean shifting responsibilities from existing roles, most commonly Operations or Program Management.

This can be confusing for both your Operations team and your clients. I like to keep the distinction simple:

  • Customer Success owns the customer relationship. They’re the liaison between the customer, their stakeholders, and the company. They make sure the customer knows who to contact, commitments are being met, contracts and renewals are managed, and the relationship continues to grow.
  • Operations owns the delivery relationship. They’re the liaison between the service, product, or program being delivered and the customer’s point of contact. They make sure delivery is running smoothly, teams are aligned, and the agreed-upon service is being executed.

Responsibilities will overlap, and that’s okay. When introducing a CSM to a client, make it clear there’s no wrong person to contact. Operations and CS work together to get each request into the right hands.

Both teams should communicate regularly and use a shared source of truth, whether that’s a customer relationship management (CRM) system, project management tool, or centralized account documentation. Both teams should be able to see:

  • Contract details, scope, and renewal dates.
  • Customer contacts, stakeholders, and escalation paths.
  • Customer goals, expectations, and commitments, including what was promised about the AI.
  • Operational performance, KPIs, and service level agreements (SLAs).
  • Open issues, risks, and action items.
  • Upcoming changes, projects, and expansion opportunities.

Done well, adding a CSM doesn’t create more handoffs. It gets everyone working from the same plan.

Where should Customer Success report? There’s no single answer. In Gainsight’s 2025 index, CS reports to the CEO at 28% of companies, to a Chief Customer Officer at 25%, to the head of sales at 25%, and to the COO or President at 17%. A CCO is far more common at larger companies (35% over $50 million in ARR versus 3% to 4% under $20 million). Reporting into Sales ties CS closely to revenue, but Gainsight’s own CRO cautions that it can pull CS toward short-term sales over long-term success. Whichever you choose, settle the charter early. Does CS own GRR, NRR, or both?

Here’s what that collaboration looks like in practice:

ScenarioCS ActionOperations Action
Customer wants to renegotiate their contractLeads the negotiation and meetingsSupports with delivery costs/capacity
SLA performance is decliningCommunicates impact and manages relationshipInvestigates and resolves performance issues
Customer is unhappy with service qualityOwns relationship recoveryCreates corrective action plan
Customer is questioning the value of the AI productUnderstands concerns, reinforces business value, and coordinates the right conversationsProvides product or technical context and helps address performance issues

Operations isn’t the only department whose responsibilities may shift when you introduce a CSM. Account Managers and Account Executives may also be affected, especially if they currently own renewals, upselling, or commercial negotiations.

Before finalizing the role, involve the relevant departments, and make it a conversation, not an announcement. Ask each department head:

  • What does Customer Success mean to you?
  • What do you expect the CSM to own?
  • What are you worried will be taken away, or left undone?

Write the answers on one page and agree on it together. Make sure everyone understands what the CSM owns, what stays with existing roles, and where responsibilities overlap. You don’t want two people assuming the other owns an important part of the customer relationship, and you don’t want your CSM trying to solve every problem alone.

The Compensation

CSM compensation depends on the expectations of the role, its potential ROI, and how you’ll measure success.

As a starting point, CSM compensation often includes a base salary and variable pay (bonus). An 80/20 split is one option, with 80% base and 20% variable.

Some common ways to bonus CSMs include:

  • Gross Revenue Retention (GRR)
  • Net Revenue Retention (NRR)
  • Renewal rate
  • Expansion revenue
  • Customer adoption
  • Customer satisfaction (CSAT)
  • Overall company performance

This is a starting point, not a rule. The right structure depends on your company’s needs and priorities. Tie compensation to responsibilities and outcomes the CSM can actually influence.

Who should your first CSM be?

Don’t confuse a founding CSM with an entry-level one. Your first Customer Success hire isn’t just managing accounts. They’re setting up the workflows, templates, scorecards, and habits everyone after them will follow, usually with no existing team to learn from. That takes someone senior, or at least experienced enough to have seen a Success function work and to build one from scratch.

A mid-level CSM can be a good fit if someone with Customer Success experience is guiding them, such as a founder, advisor, or leader who has built a team before. Entry-level CSMs fit best later, once the playbooks and processes exist for them to follow.

What are CSMs paid?

The CS Pulse analyzed 2,710 Customer Success job postings in late 2026, about 550 of which listed a salary. The overall median was $90,000. Here are the posted ranges by level, rounded:

LevelPosted salary rangeWhere it fits at an AI startup
Entry-level CSM$62K–$79KLater, once playbooks and processes exist for them to follow
Mid-level$91K–$123KYour first hire only if an experienced leader or advisor is guiding them
Senior$116K–$172KThe usual fit for a first or founding CSM
Director$140K–$183KWhen you’re building a department, not a first hire

Source: The CS Pulse salary report. These are posted job-listing ranges, not actual pay. Equity and bonus aren’t included, the report doesn’t say whether the ranges are percentiles, and it isn’t broken out by company stage or AI companies. Pay varies a lot by city. Use it as a starting point and check it against current postings for your market.

The Job Description

Now you’re ready to write the job description. And hey, we’re living in the future, so you can use AI to help draft it.

Below is a prompt you can give your favorite large language model (LLM). Add as much context as you can so it understands your business and what you need from the role.

Prompt

Act as an experienced Head of Customer Success who specializes in building CS teams for growing businesses and SaaS companies, particularly AI companies.

I want you to help me create a Customer Success Manager job description based on my company’s needs, goals, and current organizational structure.

Use the information below to define the role. Don’t default to a generic CSM job description. I want you to think critically about what this person should own and how their success should be measured.

1. About the business

Company name and industry:

What our product or service does:

Business model (SaaS, B2B, B2C, etc.):

Customer profile and typical contract value:

Number of customers and current ARR (if applicable):

2. Why we’re building a CS team

What problems are we trying to solve?

What are our biggest customer retention, adoption, or growth challenges?

Why are we hiring this role now?

Are customers struggling to understand or adopt our AI product?

Are customers comparing our solution to competitors or considering building their own?

Are there opportunities to expand into other departments or use cases?

3. What success looks like

Our primary business goals:

KPIs we’ll use to measure success (GRR, NRR, churn, renewals, expansion, adoption, CSAT, etc.):

Current baseline and target metrics, if available:

What business outcomes should customers achieve using our product?

How will we measure AI adoption and value realization?

4. Role ownership and responsibilities

What responsibilities will the CSM own?

What responsibilities will remain with Operations, Account Management, Sales, or Support?

Where will responsibilities overlap?

Will the CSM own renewals, upselling, or commercial negotiations?

What internal teams will they work with?

Will the CSM be responsible for educating customers about AI capabilities and limitations?

Will they be expected to identify new use cases or expansion opportunities across departments?

What level of technical or AI knowledge will the role require?

Will they manage relationships with executive sponsors as well as day-to-day contacts?

5. Compensation and structure

Expected base salary range:

Variable compensation or bonus structure:

Reporting manager:

Individual contributor or leadership role:

6. Additional details

Preferred experience and qualifications:

Tools and systems currently in use:

Remote, hybrid, or in-office:

Any other expectations or requirements:

Your deliverables:

Recommend the appropriate job title and level based on the responsibilities, rather than defaulting to Customer Success Manager.

Identify any gaps, conflicting responsibilities, or unrealistic expectations in my proposed role.

Create a clear job description with an overview, key responsibilities, required qualifications, and preferred qualifications.

Include 30/60/90-day expectations for the new hire.

Recommend measurable performance goals and KPIs that align with the business challenges I’ve identified.

Suggest a compensation structure that aligns with the role’s responsibilities and the outcomes they can influence.

Consider the AI-specific responsibilities that may be relevant to this company, including customer education, AI adoption, product differentiation, value realization, stakeholder management, and expansion opportunities.

Before drafting the job description, ask me any important follow-up questions you need answered. If information is missing, don’t make assumptions. Help me build a role that makes sense for my business, not just another generic CSM job posting.

You don’t have to fill everything out perfectly. Give the AI enough context to create a first draft, then review it, make adjustments, and add your personal touch.

Hiring and onboarding usually belong to your People or HR team, so this guide leaves them out. Hand them the job description you just wrote and the first-90-days plan in the next chapter.

Mapping Your Customer Journey

Before building new processes, take a look at the ones you already have.

One of the first projects for your Customer Success team should be mapping the customer journey, from contract signature through onboarding, deployment, adoption, renewal, and expansion. I’ve created a Customer Journey Survey CSMs can use to audit the process.

I’d make this one of your CSM’s first projects once they’ve had time to learn the product. It’s a great way to meet people across the organization, understand how teams work together, and spot ways to improve the customer experience.

CSMs bring value here, too. They help teams see what’s working, uncover gaps, and make sure each stage of the customer journey has clear ownership.

The First 90 Days

A new CSM needs a plan, so let’s answer “what does success look like in the first 90 days?”

DaysFocusWhat the CSM doesWhat you can measure
1–30LearnInterview five customers with one question: “What does success look like for you?” Learn the product. Meet Sales, Operations, Support, and Product. Read the history on your top accounts. Sit in on customer calls. Get introduced to key contacts.Accounts reviewed, introductions made, baseline metrics recorded
31–60MapRun the Customer Journey Survey and turn the No answers into action items. Build a Customer Health Scorecard for the top accounts. Start Mutual Success Plans. Begin sending weekly updates.Survey completed, action items assigned, scorecards and plans in place
61–90ActHold the first business reviews. Close the top action items. Run a renewal risk review. Share baseline numbers and early wins with leadership.Business reviews held, risks flagged, first results reported

Customer Journey Survey

Use the questions below to guide conversations with internal teams. Mark each one Yes, No, or N/A. Note how the process works and who owns it. Anything missing or in need of improvement can become an action item.

Not every question will apply. Adapt the survey to your product, customers, and existing workflows.

There are 69 questions in eight sections, and the Customer Journey Audit workbook in the Resources section has all of them with space for answers, owners, and follow-ups. And it turns every gap into an action item automatically.

1. Customer information and ownership
1.01Do we have a centralized location for customer information, such as a CRM or account management platform?
1.02Is there a clearly defined owner responsible for maintaining customer records?
1.03Do internal teams know who to contact when customer information needs to be added or updated?
1.04Are customer goals, use cases, success criteria, and commitments documented?
1.05Are customer contacts, stakeholders, decision-makers, and escalation paths documented?
1.06Can relevant teams easily access the customer’s contract, scope, and renewal date?
1.07Is there a documented process for handing an account over when its owner changes?
1.08Do we document which AI features, models, or workflows each customer has purchased, enabled, or been promised?
1.09Is it clear which team owns the customer relationship and which team owns the delivery relationship?
2. Contract signature and handoff
2.01Is there a consistent process for handing a signed contract from Sales to Customer Success?
2.02Does the CSM receive the information they need before the customer kickoff?
2.03Are the customer’s goals, expectations, use cases, and any promises made during the sales process documented?
2.04Is there a clear owner for scheduling and leading the kickoff?
2.05Are internal teams notified when a new customer signs?
2.06Do Sales and CS have shared guidance on what can and cannot be promised about AI capabilities, accuracy, and timelines?
2.07Are non-standard terms (custom SLAs, pricing, data handling, usage limits) flagged to CS and Operations before signature?
3. Onboarding and implementation
3.01Is there a documented onboarding process for new customers?
3.02Are onboarding milestones, responsibilities, and timelines defined?
3.03Is there a clear owner for each implementation task?
3.04Are customer requirements and technical dependencies documented before implementation begins?
3.05Is there a process for collecting required data, credentials, and integrations securely?
3.06Are security, privacy, and compliance requirements reviewed when applicable?
3.07Are AI-specific requirements, such as data sources, intended use cases, human review, and acceptable output quality, documented?
3.08Is there a process for testing the solution and confirming readiness before launch?
3.09Do we define what successful onboarding and deployment look like?
3.10Is there a process for communicating delays, blockers, or changes in scope to the customer?
3.11Do we capture the customer’s baseline (for example, current time spent or error rates) before launch so value can be measured later?
3.12Is it clear how customer data is handled by the AI (storage, retention, deletion, and use for model training), and is this communicated to the customer?
4. Adoption and value realization
4.01Do we have a defined process for helping customers adopt the product after deployment?
4.02Are customer training and education responsibilities clearly assigned?
4.03Do we track whether customers are using the product’s key features or workflows?
4.04Do we have a way to identify customers who are underusing the product or struggling to get value?
4.05Do we regularly review progress against the customer’s original goals and success criteria?
4.06Is there a process for collecting feedback about AI output quality, accuracy, or reliability when relevant?
4.07Do we help customers understand the product’s capabilities and limitations?
4.08Is there a clear process for identifying and documenting new use cases?
4.09Do we measure value delivered (for example, hours saved, cost reduced, or accuracy improved) and not just usage?
4.10Is there a documented Customer Health Scorecard, and a defined action when a score drops?
5. Support, issues, and escalations
5.01Do customers know where to go when they need help?
5.02Is there a documented process for routing customer issues to the right team?
5.03Are escalation paths and response expectations clearly defined?
5.04Is there a process for tracking unresolved issues and communicating updates to customers?
5.05Are recurring issues reviewed with Product, Engineering, or Operations?
5.06Is there a process for communicating product incidents or changes that may affect customers?
5.07Is there a process for reporting AI-specific issues (incorrect, biased, or unsafe outputs) and routing them to Product or Engineering?
5.08During an incident, is it clear who owns the customer conversation and who owns the fix?
6. Renewals and account growth
6.01Is there a documented renewal process with clear ownership?
6.02Are CSMs automatically notified of upcoming renewals, ideally 60–90 days in advance?
6.03Are customers notified of upcoming renewals according to a defined timeline?
6.04Is there a process for reviewing customer health and renewal risk before the renewal date?
6.05Is there a clear process for identifying and qualifying expansion opportunities?
6.06When a customer wants to expand a program or add a use case, is it clear who owns the demo, pricing, pipeline entry, proposal, contract, and follow-through?
6.07Is there a process for handing expansion opportunities to Sales or Account Management when appropriate?
6.08Are annual price increases and renewal terms tracked, with a clear owner making sure they are applied?
6.09Is there a process for spotting customers who may switch to another AI tool or build their own solution in-house?
6.10Do we look for expansion opportunities beyond the department that originally purchased?
6.11Is there a process for identifying happy customers and collecting references, testimonials, and case studies?
7. Internal collaboration and communication
7.01Do CS, Sales, Operations, Support, and Product meet regularly to discuss customer accounts?
7.02Is there a shared source of truth that all teams use for contract details, risks, open issues, and action items?
7.03Are responsibilities for CS, Operations, Sales or Account Management, and Support documented, including where they overlap?
7.04Do internal teams understand what the CSM role owns and when to involve a CSM?
7.05Is there a process for CS to share customer feedback and feature requests with Product, and for Product to close the loop?
7.06Is there a process for CS to raise customer risks (churn, escalations, executive concerns) to leadership?
7.07Are the CS team’s success metrics defined, and do other teams know what they are?
8. AI-specific considerations
8.01Do we have a documented position on the AI’s limitations, expected accuracy, and responsible use that customers can see?
8.02Is there a process for answering customer questions about how the AI works, data security, and model changes?
8.03Do we monitor AI output quality over time, not just at launch?
8.04Do we tell customers about model updates or changes in AI behavior when they happen?
8.05Is there a clear owner for AI quality or accuracy issues raised by customers?

Once the answers are in, a chart like this shows you where the gaps are at a glance. The sections with the most No answers are your first priorities.

But what good are these answers without action?

Use the results to build an improvement plan. Identify what needs to be defined or refined, assign an owner and due date to each action item, and agree on how you’ll follow up.

In my template, answering “No” automatically adds an action item to a separate tab, where you can assign an owner and due date. It’s probably my favorite resource in this guide.

Defining the Customer Lifecycle

Customer Success needs a repeatable way to guide customers from contract signature to ongoing value. The survey and follow-up actions should give you a clearer view of your current customer lifecycle. A typical lifecycle looks like this:

Document your current process, define each stage, and identify its owner (including their title and email address). Keep this as a living internal reference for new hires and as teams change.

Tools, Software, and Solutions for Success

Your audit may have uncovered gaps in how customer information is maintained. For example:

  • Calls aren’t recorded, or recordings aren’t stored somewhere the team can access.
  • Everyone uses a different note-taking tool, so finding call notes means checking four or five websites.
  • A customer expressed interest in expanding services, but there’s no shared record of the opportunity, its status, or who owns the next step.
  • Renewals are inconsistent because reminders aren’t being sent.

The list goes on.

These are process problems the right tools can help solve. Before buying anything, review the software you already use. It may be able to meet your needs, or let you consolidate tools instead of adding another one.

Aim for a connected system where customer information is easy to find, conversations are documented, and teams know what needs to happen next.

Tools change fast. The names below are examples, not endorsements, and some of them will be different by the time you read this. Check each vendor’s current features and pricing.

You won’t need every category on day one. This table shows examples of each and what to add as the team grows:

CRM and Centralized Customer Information

Your CRM should be the central source of truth for customer and account information such as key contacts, account history, contract details, renewal dates, opportunities, and important interactions. Anyone working with an account should be able to answer:

  • Who are the key stakeholders?
  • What did we agree to deliver?
  • What are the customer’s goals and current priorities?
  • What opportunities, risks, or open action items exist?
  • Who owns the next step?

Choose a system that can use contract dates to trigger renewal tasks, assign them to the right owner, and log activity to the customer record. And avoid scattering critical customer information across spreadsheets, personal notes, and inboxes. If it matters to the account, it belongs in a shared system.

What to watch for with everything else

  • Customer Success platforms build on CRM data. A smaller team can usually manage in its CRM until the need for a dedicated platform is clear.
  • Call recording: standardize on one approved tool and define where recordings and notes live. Confirm recording consent, access permissions, and retention policies before rolling it out.
  • Knowledge base: assign owners to key documents and review them regularly so outdated instructions don’t become the default.
  • Project tracking: don’t add another task system unless it solves a real coordination problem.
  • Chat: it’s convenient, but it shouldn’t be the only place customer information lives. Capture key decisions, risks, and action items in your CRM.
  • Feedback and reporting: someone has to review survey responses and close the loop, and your data should be reliable before you invest in dashboards.
  • Vendor consolidation: your tool vendors can be acquired, too. Gartner’s March 2026 review of voice-of-the-customer platforms notes that one leading vendor announced plans to buy another that had just acquired a third, and warns that consolidation can increase vendor dependency and reduce buyers’ negotiating leverage. Before you commit, ask about contract length, data export, and what happens to your terms if the vendor is acquired.

Large Language Model (LLM)

An LLM can help your CS team get more out of the information it already has. I’m sure by now we’re all using them for summarizing calls, but we can also summarize account history, draft follow-ups and QBRs, turn meeting notes into action items, find themes in survey responses, and review a Mutual Success Plan for missing owners or dates. With the right integrations, it can also help employees find answers across approved company knowledge sources.

Treat AI output as a first draft and add your personal touch. I always say being able to sound human is an advantage today. Review it for accuracy, and never enter confidential customer or company information into an unapproved tool. Follow your organization’s data security and privacy policies.

You’re not alone if you’re still figuring this out. In Gainsight’s 2025 index, 52% of CS teams use AI (up from 44% a year earlier), but most are early. Of those, 63% have an initial rollout with limited use cases and only 2% say AI is fully embedded. The most common uses save time, such as auto-summarizing (82% of adopters) and drafting follow-ups (71%). Churn and risk prediction is the next step, with 39% adopting it and 77% exploring it. The top barrier is output reliability (50%, up 10 points), followed by integration complexity (45%) and lack of in-house expertise (39%). Fewer than 5% of respondents have deployed AI agents.

A practical order is to start with summaries and drafts, then move to risk signals once your customer data is clean. Be skeptical of time-savings claims, like the 15 to 20 minutes per call summary Gainsight’s CTO cites. They’re vendor-reported, not survey results, so test them on your own calls.

Maintaining Relationships

Here’s what you’ve done so far:

  • You made the case for adding a CS team!
  • You built a job description around your business and customer needs.
  • You mapped the customer journey, filled in gaps, and defined ownership.
  • You chose the tools to keep customer information in one place.

Take a moment. That’s a lot!

Now that you’ve built the foundation, it’s time for your CS team to find its rhythm with their accounts.

Onboarding Your Customers

How a customer’s first 30 to 60 days go often decides how the next year goes. With an AI product, onboarding shapes what the customer expects. If they think the AI will be perfect on day one, even a good launch will feel like a letdown.

Define “first value” before you start. Pick one result the customer cares about that you can reach quickly, such as “the AI resolves 20% of tickets without a human” or “reports are ready in an hour instead of a day.” Everything in onboarding points toward it.

Speed matters. Focus Digital’s 2026 churn report says 43% of SMB customer losses happen in the first 90 days, and Liat Benzur describes a “spike-and-fade” pattern with AI tools, where heavy use in the first month is followed by abandonment. A fast first win and an early usage check-in are cheap protection.

PhaseWhat happens
Before kickoffThe CSM reviews the sales handoff: goals, promises made, and anything unusual in the contract. Capture the customer’s baseline (current time spent, error rates) so you can show improvement later.
KickoffAgree on the first-value goal, the timeline, who does what, and what data and integrations are needed. Say plainly what the AI will do well, what it won’t, and how much human review to expect at first.
Setup and launchTest the solution before it goes live. Start with a limited rollout and human review before going all in. Train the people who will use it.
First 30 to 60 daysCheck usage and output quality weekly and fix problems fast. Write down the first win and share it with the customer’s sponsor. Then move into the Mutual Success Plan cadence.

Here’s where AI onboarding tends to go wrong:

  • Expecting perfect accuracy on day one. Set expectations early and show how quality improves. Underpromise and over-deliver, wink wink.
  • Messy or missing data. Find out in the first week, not the third month.
  • No owner on the customer side. Name a champion, and ask who might be worried about what AI means for their job.
  • Scope growing during implementation. Agree on what’s in the first release and what comes later.

Track Time to Value (TTV), onboarding completion rate, and time to first key outcome. They’re already in your metrics table.

Using AI

Paste your handoff notes, contract summary, and the customer’s goals into your LLM and ask: “Draft a kickoff agenda, and list anything promised during the sales process that we haven’t documented.”

Mutual Success Plan

So, what’s a Mutual Success Plan?

It may go by several different names, including Mutual Action Plan or Joint Success Plan. Whatever you call it, it’s a living document that the Customer Success Manager and customer build and maintain together.

The plan uses your customer lifecycle as a starting point, but reflects each customer’s goals, priorities, responsibilities, and timeline. The CSM and customer should revisit it, update it as things change, and use it to stay aligned.

A Mutual Success Plan isn’t necessary for every customer. Use your judgment based on account size, complexity, and strategic importance. A simple action list may be enough for some customers while larger or more complex accounts may benefit from a shared plan.

The plan also gives your CSM a reason to get nosy. Beyond the goals of their main contact or department, it can uncover broader company priorities and opportunities to support other teams or initiatives.

The plan should capture:

  • Customer goals and desired outcomes
  • Key milestones and target dates
  • Action items, owners, and deadlines
  • Customer and CSM responsibilities
  • Risks, blockers, and dependencies
  • Progress toward success and value realization

Keep the plan somewhere both parties can access, such as your CS platform or a shared document. The customer and CSM should be the primary editors, with internal stakeholders given view access as needed. Store it in your central customer database so the wider team has context, and use it to prepare for business reviews and internal 1:1s.

Using AI

Paste the plan into your LLM (with customer-confidential details removed if your policy requires it) and ask: “List every action item that has no owner or no due date, and flag any customer goal that has no action item connected to it.”

I created a sample Mutual Success Plan you can download and adapt for your own team. It’s pretty awesome, and it’s a good place to start.

Introductions and Communication Cadence

A strong customer relationship starts with a thoughtful introduction. That might seem obvious, but I have organized a warm intro where the coworker I was introducing just started yammering off discovery questions without setting expectations or allowing the customer to properly introduce themselves. Here’s how I’d get myself acquainted with a new face:

1. Get a warm introduction

Ask someone who already works regularly with the customer to introduce you to the key stakeholders. A warm introduction from a familiar face makes it easier to build trust. Then book a dedicated Customer Success call and keep the invitation brief, with an agenda so the customer knows what to expect and why the meeting is worth their time.

2. Prepare before the call

Research the company, review the account history, and talk with internal teams who work with the customer. Use what you learn to prefill the Mutual Success Plan before the meeting. This helps you ask informed questions instead of making the customer repeat information they’ve already shared. (Something my coworker should’ve done before the call.)

3. Make the first Success call count

Use the call to:

  • Introduce yourself and explain your role in their account.
  • Share how they can make the best use of you and the Customer Success team.
  • Build rapport with a little small talk.
  • Review the Mutual Success Plan together.
  • Confirm or update their goals, priorities, stakeholders, responsibilities, and milestones.

Give the customer room to correct what you’ve gathered or fill in the gaps. The plan should reflect their priorities, not just your internal assumptions.

Get to know your main contact’s manager or executive sponsor, too. AI can bring skepticism and competing priorities, so you may need to build that relationship over time. Keep your primary contact in the loop if you reach out to their boss in the future. Address your contact directly and copy their manager when it makes sense. Make the work visible and collaborative, not a way around your contact. I always liked asking, “What can I do to make you look good?” Helping your contact show the value they’re bringing to the business is part of the partnership. It’s also why I recommend inviting their manager to business reviews.

For an AI company, ask which AI tools they’ve implemented, how those tools are working for them, and where they’re considering using AI next.

Send a recap the same day or by the next morning with the updated Mutual Success Plan, and the next meeting date. That gives both sides a shared record and a clear path forward.

4. Set your cadence and channel

Recommend a recurring meeting cadence based on the account’s needs, complexity, and current stage. Explain your reasoning and invite the customer to adjust it.

At a previous job, I held weekly syncs with every new account for its first month, and it worked well. That gave the customer dedicated time with me while questions and action items were coming up. After that, I moved to monthly or twice-monthly meetings based on the account. Meet more often during implementation, major changes, or periods of risk, and less often when the account is stable.

A weekly update is not a meeting, and it’s not a business review. It’s a short note by email or Slack that keeps the client in the loop. Here’s how the pieces fit together:

TypeHow oftenWhoPurposeFormat
Weekly updateWeekly, ongoingCSM to the main contactKeep the client in the loop: what happened, what’s coming, and anything you need from themA short email or Slack note, no meeting
Sync callWeekly for the first month, then monthly or twice a monthCSM and the main contactQuestions, action items, and Mutual Success Plan progress15 to 30 minute call
Monthly business reviewMonthlyCSM, Operations, and the customer’s main contactProgress, challenges, and anything that needs attentionShort call with a few key numbers
Quarterly business review (QBR)QuarterlyCSM, Operations, the main contact, and their manager or executive sponsorThe partnership as a whole: results, ROI, risks, and next quarter’s planLonger meeting with an agenda and slides

Ask how the customer prefers to communicate between meetings, whether that’s Slack or email, and be clear about which questions belong where and what response times to expect.

And no one likes a pointless calendar invite. Send an agenda, track action items, and share notes afterward. If the customer consistently has little to discuss, revisit the cadence instead of keeping meetings on the calendar out of habit.

Customer Health Scorecard

A Customer Health Scorecard is an internal view of how an account is performing and whether the customer is getting value from your product or service. It brings together signals from across the relationship to show which accounts are healthy, which need attention, and where there may be room to grow.

A useful scorecard can give you psychic abilities and help you spot risk before the customer even raises a concern.

And no, it shouldn’t just measure whether the customer likes you. Sure, sentiment matters, but it’s only one input.

A customer might love their CSM, attend every meeting, and respond to every email, but still not get the results they expected. Another customer might be quiet, rarely attend meetings, and need very little hand-holding while getting tremendous value from your solution.

If you’re only measuring the relationship, you’re missing half the picture.

Building Your Scorecard

For an AI company, I’d build the scorecard around five key areas:

Product Performance and Outcomes

Is the product actually doing what it’s supposed to do?

Usage and automation numbers can look impressive on paper without translating into a good customer experience.

Look at the performance of the AI, how accurately it’s completing its intended tasks, and whether it’s delivering the business outcomes promised. Metrics like AI resolution rate, cost per resolution, and containment (the share of requests the AI handles without a human) can tell a bigger story.

Adoption and Engagement

Are they actually using what they’ve purchased?

A customer can have a fantastic product with all the bells and whistles, but if they’re only using a fraction of its capabilities, they may not be getting the full value of their investment.

For an AI company, I’d look at how much of the customer’s eligible volume is being handled by the AI, how many workflows have been deployed, and whether adoption is expanding across the channels or departments identified in their success plan.

I’d also look at whether the customer is participating in training, optimization sessions, and other activities that help them get more out of the product. A lot of times, customers aren’t getting notified when new updates are happening (or they did, but forget and need a reminder.)

Relationship Health

Are you maintaining relationships with the right people? Do you have access to decision-makers? Are customers comfortable bringing concerns to you? And perhaps most importantly, do you know what’s happening within their organization?

This is where you learn if they actually like and trust your company and the people involved.

Don’t rely solely on how you feel a relationship is going. Look at the actual engagement and feedback you’re receiving. While a customer might not have anything against you personally, a customer ignoring emails and not showing up to calls has low engagement regardless.

And a customer showing up to calls, but coming with a list of complaints might have high engagement, but the happy sentiment isn’t there.

Operational Health

This is where you need to get your Operations, Technical Support, and Product teams involved.

Is the customer experiencing recurring technical issues? Are integrations reliable? Are escalations being resolved in a reasonable amount of time? Are there outstanding blockers preventing the customer from getting the results they expected?

Sometimes the customer relationship is perfectly fine, but the operational side of the account is struggling. Your CSM might be doing everything right, but if the product isn’t working as expected, that will eventually affect the customer’s perception of your company.

Commercial and Business Health

Finally, what’s happening with the customer’s business, and how does it affect your relationship?

A customer might be getting excellent results from your product, but if they’ve experienced budget cuts, a change in leadership, or a shift in company priorities, their renewal could still be at risk.

This is also where you can identify opportunities for growth. Are there additional departments that could benefit from your solution? Has the customer expressed interest in expanding services? Are there new initiatives that align with what you offer?

Next, decide how you’ll score the metrics that matter to your business.

Start with a weighted scoring model. Not every category should carry the same weight. For an AI company, product performance and adoption may matter more than meeting attendance. Score each area, multiply by its weight, and add them up.

A 0–100 scale is one option, with three health categories:

  • Green (80–100): Healthy. The customer is achieving value, adoption is progressing, and there are no significant unresolved concerns.
  • Yellow (50–79): Needs attention. There are gaps in adoption, engagement, performance, or customer sentiment that need follow-up.
  • Red (0–49): At risk. There are significant concerns that could affect retention or the customer’s ability to achieve their goals.

These thresholds are a starting point. Adjust them based on your customer data and experience. Here’s what a finished scorecard can look like for a Conglom-O customer, Strickland Propane:

Turn the Score Into Action

A Customer Health Scorecard is only useful if you act on it. Rally the right people and create an action-item list. Immediately assign an owner and due date to each item… I’m serious, do not call that action-item list done until everyone knows what is expected of them.

Document the risks, actions taken, and outcomes. Over time, this gives your team a record of what’s working, where customers get stuck, and how to prevent similar issues.

Customer health is a team effort. The CSM may own the scorecard, but improving account health often takes Operations, Technical Support, Product, Finance, and other teams. Bring in the right people and keep them in the loop.

Don’t worry about getting the scoring model perfect on the first try. You can keep refining it as your customer base grows and you learn more about what drives retention, adoption, and expansion.

Pay attention to the scores. If nearly every account is green, your criteria may be too lenient. If nearly every account is red, you may be weighting some categories too heavily. Use actual customer outcomes to keep calibrating the model.

Choose signals that move early. Focus Digital’s report says product usage falls an average of 41% in the quarter before a customer cancels, and that voluntary churn starts to accelerate about 90 days out. The method isn’t published, so verify it against your own data, but it’s a good reason to track usage trends over time and not just a score at one moment. Gainsight’s index also found 72% of teams use a customer health score as a primary non-revenue metric, while NPS fell from 69% to 53%. Gainsight explains that NPS is a snapshot and misses day-to-day sentiment.

I’ve included an Excel-based Customer Health Scorecard under Resources that you can use or adapt as a starting point. Any time a score drops to yellow or red, an action item is automatically created.
