Establishing Business Reviews

Business reviews are an important part of maintaining a healthy customer relationship. I recommend holding a quarterly business review (QBR) at a minimum, but don’t wait three months to talk to your customers. Keep them in the loop with a short weekly update, hold a monthly business review to discuss progress, challenges, and anything that needs attention, and save the bigger conversation for the QBR.

The weekly update is not a business review. It’s a quick email or Slack note with operational updates and performance scores, and it doesn’t need a business review format (but do whatever moves you). Refer to the table in Introductions and Communication Cadence to see how it all works.

A good business review doesn’t just read off scores or walk through a few slides. Your CSM is there to tell the full story. It should highlight progress, uncover risks, identify opportunities for expansion, and give both sides a chance to talk about what’s working and what could be better.

I recommend scheduling QBRs at least a month in advance. This gives your customer time to prioritize the meeting and gives you an opportunity to reinforce its importance. This helps most with customers who aren’t always eager to attend business reviews.

Invite your main point of contact and their manager or executive sponsor. You should also be thoughtful about who joins from your own team. A colleague shared with me the rule of bringing one more person than the customer does. If they invite one person, bring two. If they invite two, bring three. It’s a simple way to keep the meeting balanced while making sure the right people are in the room.

I’d have the CSM and someone from Operations attend every time. If the customer brings a director or executive, consider bringing someone at a similar level from your own organization. Having a Director of Operations or another senior leader join can show that your company takes the partnership seriously and is invested in its success.

What to Include in a Business Review

Use your Mutual Success Plan as a starting point for the agenda. It gives you a natural way to revisit the customer’s goals, review progress, and make sure everyone is still aligned. Here’s a sample 60-minute agenda:

SegmentMinutesWho leadsWhat to cover
Welcome and recap5CSMConfirm the agenda and revisit the customer’s original goals
Business objectives and progress10CSMMutual Success Plan review: what’s done, what’s outstanding, and blockers
Product performance10OperationsPerformance, accuracy, trends, and recurring issues, then ask for feedback
Business impact and ROI10CSM and customerTime or money saved, workload reduced, and the customer’s own numbers
Challenges, feedback, and open issues10CSM and OperationsWhat’s not working and exactly what happens next
Next quarter’s action plan10CSMNew goals, milestones, and renewal timing
Company updates and wrap-up5CSMNew features, integrations, and milestones, then confirm owners and dates

Here are the areas I’d recommend covering:

Business Objectives and Progress

Revisit the customer’s original business objectives and the action items you agreed to work on. What has been completed? Celebrate the wins. What is still outstanding? Talk about blockers and what needs to happen next.

Product Performance

Review how the product is performing and whether it’s meeting expectations. Having someone from Operations involved helps here. They can speak to performance, accuracy, recurring issues, and any operational trends.

Don’t just present the numbers. Ask for feedback. If performance is strong, this may also be an opportunity to discuss what else the product could help them accomplish.

Business Impact and ROI

Good performance numbers don’t tell you whether the customer’s business improved. Ask about the impact the product is having on their business. Has it saved time or money? Reduced workload? Improved efficiency? Identify measurable outcomes wherever possible.

Challenges, Feedback, and Open Issues

Discuss recurring issues, technical blockers, and customer feedback. More importantly, explain what you’re doing about them.

You don’t need to have an immediate fix for every problem, but you should always leave the customer knowing what happens next. If you sell AI Agents and a client complains that it is consistently giving incorrect answers, acknowledge that it needs to be addressed, identify who you’re working with internally, and give the customer a timeline for your next update.

Don’t leave a customer with a problem and no plan.

Next Quarter’s Action Plan

Now that you’ve reviewed the previous quarter, talk about what’s coming next. Are the customer’s business objectives still the same? Have their priorities changed? Are there upcoming deadlines, new initiatives, or opportunities to get more value from the product?

Revisit any milestones or performance goals you’re working toward together. If a renewal is coming up next quarter, this is also a good time to discuss it and make sure there are no surprises.

Company Updates

I also like to include a slide for company-wide updates. These don’t necessarily need to be specific to the customer. Share new product features, team or leadership changes, new integrations, or other company milestones. Even if a customer doesn’t use a particular CRM integration, for example, it’s still helpful for them to see that your product and company are continuing to grow.

Make It a Conversation

One of the biggest mistakes you can make during a business review is treating it like a presentation. Nothing is more painful than watching a presenter end every slide with, “Does anyone have any questions?” You might get a polite no, and that’s the end of the conversation.

Instead, invite your customer to participate throughout the meeting. Share what you’ve noticed, explain what you’re thinking, and ask for their perspective. Try phrases like, “We noticed this trend and would love to hear your thoughts,” or “We’ve been looking at ways to improve this. What would make the biggest difference for your team?”

You want customers to feel comfortable sharing feedback, asking questions, and challenging ideas. The best business reviews are conversations, not presentations.

Don’t wait until the week of the QBR to start putting everything together. I recommend having a complete draft ready at least one week before the meeting. Use the remaining time to review it with your internal team, practice the presentation, and identify any gaps or risks.

Rehearsing also gives you a chance to anticipate questions and make sure everyone is comfortable with the information they’re presenting. If you uncover an issue during preparation, you have time to investigate it and come to the meeting with a plan. You don’t want to discover a problem for the first time while you’re presenting to the customer.

Your customer should leave the meeting feeling informed, confident in the partnership, and clear on what happens next.

The QBR Template in the Resources section has a prep timeline, an agenda, and space for metrics and next steps. (Just another awesome tool by yours truly.)

Get the QBR Template

Running a Renewal

Renewals are where all that relationship work turns into revenue. The good news is that a renewal should never be a surprise. If you’ve been running business reviews and tracking the Customer Health Scorecard, you already know how the conversation will go before it starts.

Start earlier than feels necessary. I’d begin about 120 days before the contract end date, and no later than 90, so you have time to fix problems before they become the reason someone doesn’t renew.

WhenWhat happens
120 days outPull the contract. Confirm the end date, the price increase terms, and what the customer bought. Review the Customer Health Scorecard and open action items.
90 days outBuild a short renewal plan. Align internally with Sales or Account Management and Operations on who leads, what you’ll offer, and any risks. Fix what you can.
60 days outHold the renewal conversation. Recap the value the customer has received (use their numbers, not yours) and explain any price increase.
30 days outSend the renewal paperwork and get the contract moving. Confirm who signs.
SignedRecord the outcome in the CRM, thank the customer, and note what you learned.
If it’s lostHold a short review within two weeks: why it happened, and what your playbooks should say next time.

Know who leads. Agree up front whether the CSM, an Account Manager, or Sales owns the negotiation. Whoever it is, the CSM should be in the room. A renewal fails when two people each assume the other has it.

Lead with value, not the invoice. Open with what the customer achieved, then get to the price. If you can’t point to a result, you have a bigger problem than the renewal, and that’s what the early start is for.

Price increases. If your contracts include an annual increase, put it in the renewal plan from day one. At my last job, I can’t tell you how many times a customer was not aware of what their increase actually was. Contacts change, and the person who originally signed the contract may have left, so make sure they have visibility. Explain it with the value the customer has seen. A clear explanation with enough notice goes far better than a surprise on the invoice.

Expect pushback, and prepare for it:

What you hearWhat to do
“It’s too expensive.”Go back to the value they’ve received. Ask what budget they’re comparing it to. Consider scaling the solution down before losing the customer.
“We could build this ourselves.”Ask what they’ve tried. Compare the real cost of building, running, and maintaining it with what they pay you.
“We’re not really using it.”This is an adoption problem. Offer training, a refreshed plan, and a usage target before talking price.
“Our budget got cut.”Ask about timing and priorities. Offer a smaller scope or a different term.
“Our champion left.”Find the new owner fast, and run the first-call steps again.

For AI companies, expect the question “why not just use ChatGPT or Claude directly?” Be ready with a concrete answer about what your product does that a general model doesn’t, and what it would cost them to replace it.

Expect questions about contract length. Liat Benzur argues that annual AI contracts can become stranded costs because tools change so fast, and that buyers increasingly want shorter commitments, pricing tied to outcomes, and the ability to export their data and prompts. That’s one writer’s opinion, not research, but it matches pushback you may hear. Be ready with options, such as a quarterly check-in with the right to adjust scope, a usage or outcome-based component, or a clear roadmap of what the customer gets during the term.

Watch for ownership changes. AI is consolidating quickly. Crunchbase counted 195 acquisitions of AI startups by other venture-backed AI companies through September 29, 2026, 14% more than in all of 2025. A smaller group of repeat buyers drives much of it, with 67 repeat buyers making about 42% of tracked deals over three years. Only publicly reported deals are counted. For CS, this means a customer’s budget owner or champion can change after an acquisition, and a competitor of yours may be bought, too. Add “ownership change” to your renewal risk review.

Putting It All Together: A Strickland Propane Story

Here’s how the pieces of this guide fit together, using two very big, well-known companies. Conglom-O sells an AI Dispatch Assistant, and Strickland Propane signs a $120,000 contract that renews in March 2027.

1. The handoff. Before the kickoff, Ed Bighead from Sales gives Rocko, the CSM, a handoff. Ed explains why Strickland signed with Conglom-O (cut dispatch planning time and reduce manual errors), what was promised, and who’s who. Hank Hill, the General Manager, is the executive sponsor. Enrique, the Dispatch Supervisor, is the day-to-day champion. Joe Jack, the Truck and Systems Lead, owns the technical side, and Donna, the accountant, will see every invoice. Rocko records all of them in the CRM.

2. Onboarding and the plan. Rocko and Filburt from Operations build onboarding around one first win; they’ll cut route planning from 45 minutes to 15. They record the 45-minute baseline before launch. Then Rocko and Enrique build the Mutual Success Plan together, with an owner and a date on every action.

3. The rhythm. Enrique gets a short weekly update, and Rocko holds a monthly review to check progress against the plan. Rocko also asks to meet Hank early, so the relationship doesn’t depend on one person.

4. The scorecard raises a flag. Four months in, planning time is down to 30 minutes and accuracy is solid. But the Customer Health Scorecard comes out at 65, Yellow. Only the first shift uses the tool (55% weekly active users against an 85% target), the second shift rollout is waiting on license approval, and the data team is prototyping an in-house alternative. Rocko turns each issue into an action item with an owner and a date. Hank approves the licenses, Filburt trains the second shift, and Rocko asks Joe Jack what the internal prototype is meant to solve.

5. The business review. At the QBR, the agenda follows the Mutual Success Plan. Rocko shares the progress and the scorecard findings honestly, and confirms the second shift start date with Hank. Conglom-O brings one more person than Strickland does, so the right people are in the room.

6. The renewal. About 120 days before March, Rocko pulls the contract and reviews the scorecard, which is back in Green now that the second shift is live. Ed and Rocko agree up front who leads the negotiation. Rocko opens with Strickland’s own numbers, not the price, and sends Donna the renewal terms early so the annual increase isn’t a surprise. When Joe Jack asks, “Why not just build this ourselves?” Rocko is ready with the real cost of building and maintaining it.

7. What the team learns. After the renewal, Rocko writes down what happened and how license approvals held up the second shift for weeks. That becomes a playbook for the next customer, and now the team knows to ask about licensing and approvals before launch, not after.

That’s the whole loop! The handoff, the plan, the rhythm, the scorecard, the review, the renewal, and what you learn for next time. Each step uses a piece of this guide, and each one makes the next easier.

Creating Playbooks and Feedback Loops

A playbook turns a recurring customer problem into a repeatable process. If your team keeps running into the same challenges, you shouldn’t have to figure out the solution from scratch every time.

This is one reason documenting action items throughout the customer journey is so important. Your Mutual Success Plan, Customer Health Scorecard, meeting notes, and support tickets can all help you identify recurring issues, understand how they were handled, and see what actually worked.

For example, if several customers are struggling with the same integration issue, you can look at how your team resolved it in the past and turn that knowledge into a documented process. Instead of having someone ask around or wait for another team member to explain what to do, they can open the playbook and get started.

The more consistently you document challenges, follow-ups, and outcomes, the more useful these insights become.

Using AI

Give your LLM a batch of action items and their outcomes (names removed) and ask: “Which problems came up most often, what did we try for each one, and which fixes actually worked? Draft a one-page playbook for the most common problem.”

What Should You Create Playbooks For?

Start with the challenges your team encounters most often. Some common examples for AI companies include:

  • Low product adoption
  • Declining customer satisfaction
  • Renewal risks
  • Expansion opportunities
  • Stakeholder or point-of-contact turnover
  • Unresolved integration issues
  • AI performance below target
  • Recurring accuracy or incorrect-resolution issues
  • Confusing product configurations or workflows

You don’t need a playbook for every possible scenario. Start with the problems that come up repeatedly or have a meaningful impact on the customer experience.

What triggers a playbook? Any problem that keeps repeating. You’ll find these by reviewing the action items from your Yellow and Red accounts on a regular schedule (monthly works well). If the same issue shows up across accounts, such as slow integrations, accuracy complaints, or low adoption after launch, it needs a playbook. You can skim the list yourself or give it to an LLM (with customer names removed) and ask it to group similar issues. Once a playbook exists, a Yellow or Red score that matches its warning signs is your cue to use it.

What Goes Into a Playbook?

Each playbook should give your team enough information to recognize the situation and know what to do next. I’d recommend including:

  • Warning Signs: What tells you this issue might be happening? Look at patterns you’ve noticed across accounts. For example, a customer repeatedly asking basic product questions might be a sign that they need additional training, even if they haven’t directly asked for it.
  • Discovery Questions: What should your team ask to better understand the situation? If an account is at risk of not renewing, find out why. Is it a budget issue, low adoption, unmet expectations, or are they considering another provider? Understanding the reason helps you determine the right next step. If budget is the issue, for example, there may be an opportunity to scale back the solution rather than lose the customer entirely.
  • Recommended Actions: Based on what’s worked in the past, what steps should your team take? Include the teams or individuals who may need to be involved.
  • Follow-Up and Outcomes: How should the issue be tracked, and what does a successful resolution look like? Document what worked, what didn’t, and any lessons that could help the next person handling a similar situation.

Here’s an example for one of the most common problems, low product adoption. Treat it as a starting point and fill in what you’ve learned from your own accounts.

Playbook: Low product adoptionWhat it says
Warning signsUsage is well below the level in the Mutual Success Plan. Only one team or workflow is active. Users keep asking basic questions. Training sessions go unattended. New features aren’t being used.
Discovery questionsDoes the team know what the product can do? Did the original champion leave or change roles? Is the product solving the problem they bought it for? Is something in the setup or integration blocking use? Is anyone worried about how AI will affect their job?
Recommended actionsOffer a training or optimization session. Re-confirm the customer’s goals and update the Mutual Success Plan. Pair the customer with a power user at a similar company, if you have one. Bring in Operations or Product if something is blocking use. Set a usage target and a check-in date.
Follow-up and outcomesReview usage weekly for 30 days. Record the cause and the fix in the account notes. Success is usage back at the agreed level for two months in a row. Add what you learned to this playbook.

Creating a Voice of the Customer Feedback Loop

Playbooks help your team respond to recurring challenges, but you also need a way to share those patterns with the rest of the business.

Customer Success is in a unique position to hear directly from customers about what’s working, what’s frustrating them, and what they wish the product could do. That feedback shouldn’t stay buried in meeting notes or individual customer accounts.

If customers are repeatedly reporting inaccurate AI responses, struggling with integrations, or finding configurations confusing, share those patterns with Product, Engineering, Technical Support, and leadership. A single complaint may be an isolated issue. The same complaint across multiple accounts could point to a much bigger problem.

I recommend creating a regular meeting or reporting process to review customer feedback and recurring themes. It could be a weekly or monthly meeting with the relevant departments. Your CRM, ticketing system, and centralized customer database can also help capture and organize feedback so it doesn’t get lost.

Using AI

Paste a month of customer notes and support tickets (names removed) and ask: “Group this feedback into themes, count how many accounts mention each one, and list the three themes Product should hear about first.”

Most importantly, close the loop. When feedback leads to a product improvement, process change, or resolution, document it and let the customer know. Customers want to know they’re being heard, and following up shows that their feedback actually makes a difference.

Where Should You Store Your Playbooks?

Once you’ve created a playbook, make sure it’s somewhere your team can actually find it. Your knowledge base is a great place to start. If you don’t have one set up yet, revisit the Tools, Software, and Solutions for Success section for some suggestions.

You can also use another centralized location, as long as the team knows where to find it and has access to the latest version. Keep playbooks easy to update as your product, processes, and customer needs evolve.

A playbook that nobody can find isn’t doing anyone much good.

Final Thoughts

You’ve created the foundation for your Customer Success function, but this is just the beginning. As your company grows, your CS team and processes will grow with it.

You’ll start to understand which customers need more hands-on support, how much time different accounts require, and where your CSMs are spending their time. You may eventually segment customers into strategic, enterprise, or other tiers and assign CSMs based on their needs. You’ll also get a better understanding of your team’s capacity and the return on that investment. Don’t assume that 100 accounts always require the same number of CSMs. Two companies can have the same number of customers and very different support needs.

Here’s a rough outline of how a Customer Success function tends to grow. Every company is different, so treat the stages as a guide, not a rulebook.

StageWhat it looks likeWhere to focusWhat to add
EarlyA founder and the first CSM share the accountsKnow every customer. Build the Mutual Success Plan and Customer Health Scorecard habitsCRM, call recording, templates from this guide
GrowingA few CSMs, and the founder steps back from most accountsDefine ownership with Operations. Run the Customer Journey Survey. Start business reviews and playbooksProject tracking, shared dashboards, a feedback loop
ScalingA Customer Success leader and customers split into tiersSegment customers, set capacity per CSM, and report ROICustomer Success platform, BI reporting, CS operations support

As your team becomes more established, you’ll also start noticing opportunities to work smarter. Maybe you can automate meeting reminders, make meeting preparation easier, trigger faster Customer Health Scorecard alerts, or give CSMs better insights into account activity. Pay attention to the tasks your team repeats and look for ways to make those processes more efficient.

Most importantly, keep reviewing your processes. Your customer base will change, and so will your product (AI is moving at lightning speed and your product team is trying to keep up). What works today may need to be adjusted six months from now.

Don’t build Customer Success just because you’ve grown big enough for another department. Build it because you want customers to get real results from your product.

When customers see value, they’re more likely to stay, renew, expand, and recommend your product. They become partners in your growth.

Start with the business problem you’re trying to solve. Define what success looks like, build the processes to support it, and keep learning from your customers.

Sources and Notes on the Numbers

Most statistics here come from vendor surveys and blog analyses, not peer-reviewed research. Use them to frame conversations, and replace them with your own numbers as soon as you have them.

  • Gainsight, Customer Success Index 2025. Conducted with Benchmarkit, September to October 2025, 400+ companies worldwide. Used for the CS responsibility, metrics, AI adoption, spending, reporting-line, and accounts-per-CSM figures. Gainsight sells Customer Success software and the respondents are mostly companies with a CS function, so results lean toward mature teams. Not specific to AI companies.
  • Focus Digital, Average Churn Rate by Industry SaaS: 2026 Report (Aug. 2026, updated Oct. 2026). Used for the AI price-tier retention, first-90-day, and usage-decline figures. Sources are mostly secondary, no sample size is given, and some figures in the report don’t reconcile with each other, so treat it as directional.
  • Liat Benzur, The Annual Plan Trap in AI Churn (March 2026). Used for the AI-native vs. SaaS churn comparison and the contract-length argument. The churn figures are attributed to Datafloq and ChartMogul but not linked; the rest is the author’s opinion and observation.
  • Crunchbase News, AI startup acquisitions (data through Sept. 29, 2026). Used for the acquisition counts. Covers only publicly reported deals in Crunchbase’s dataset, and prices were disclosed for only 12 of 195 deals.
  • SaaS Capital, 2026 Benchmarking Private SaaS Company Growth Rates (Research Brief 34). Annual survey of more than 1,000 private B2B SaaS companies, run in Q1 2026 on 2025 results. Used for the retention-and-growth relationship. SaaS Capital is a growth-debt lender, and the data is correlation, not cause. Not specific to AI companies.
  • Aleph and Benchmarkit, 2026 SaaS & AI Performance Benchmarks (June 2026), as summarized on Aleph’s website. Used for the median NRR and GRR figures. 342 companies overall, 230 reporting NRR, and segment sample sizes aren’t published. Aleph sells finance software, and the summary page has at least one apparent copy error, so check the original report before relying on a specific figure.
  • Gartner, Magic Quadrant for Voice of the Customer Platforms (March 2026). Used only for the point about vendor consolidation. Gartner research is licensed, so check its terms before quoting more of it.
  • The CS Pulse, Customer Success salary report (data as of Nov. 2026). Used for the salary ranges by level. Built from job postings, not surveys of actual pay, and the page has several internal inconsistencies (for example, the number of roles with salaries differs between sections), so treat the figures as approximate.

Glossary

The terms and acronyms used in this guide.

AIArtificial intelligence.
ARRAnnual recurring revenue. The yearly value of your subscription or recurring contracts.
B2B / B2CBusiness-to-business and business-to-consumer.
ChampionThe person at the customer who advocates for your product internally.
ChurnCustomers or revenue lost over a period of time.
ContainmentThe share of requests an AI handles from start to finish without a human stepping in.
CESCustomer Effort Score. A survey measure of how easy it was for the customer to get something done.
CRMCustomer relationship management. The system where customer and account information lives.
CSCustomer Success.
CSATCustomer Satisfaction score. A short survey measure of how satisfied a customer is.
CSMCustomer Success Manager.
Customer Health ScorecardAn internal view of how an account is doing, built from weighted scores across several areas.
Executive sponsorA senior person at the customer who backs the relationship and the budget.
Expansion revenueAdditional revenue from existing customers, such as upgrades, new products, users, or use cases.
GRRGross Revenue Retention. The share of revenue you keep from existing customers, not counting expansion.
KPIKey performance indicator. A metric you track to measure progress toward a goal.
LLMLarge language model. The kind of AI behind tools like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.
Logo retentionThe share of customers (not dollars) you keep over a period.
Mutual Success PlanA living plan the CSM and customer build together, with goals, milestones, owners, and deadlines.
NPSNet Promoter Score. A survey measure of how likely customers are to recommend you.
NRRNet Revenue Retention. Revenue from existing customers including expansion, minus churn and downgrades.
PlaybookA documented, repeatable response to a recurring customer situation.
QBRQuarterly business review. A meeting to review results and plan the next quarter with a customer.
ROIReturn on investment. What you gain compared to what you spend.
SaaSSoftware as a service.
SLAService level agreement. The performance and response commitments in a contract.
TTVTime to Value. How long it takes a new customer to get their first meaningful result.
